ECE 6390 / Orbits and look angles

Solar push

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how an external acceleration projects onto rotating radial and tangential axes.

Let β be the inertial direction of the solar push and θ the satellite's orbital angle. The local radial and tangential axes rotate with θ, so the force direction relative to them is β − θ.

Project the acceleration as aᵣ = aₛ cos(β − θ) and aθ = aₛ sin(β − θ). The supplied pressure convention gives aₛ = 9.08 × 10⁻⁶ αᵣ/ρₐ m/s², where ρₐ = m/A is area density in kg/m² and αᵣ is the model's reflectivity parameter.

These components enter the equations of motion as rates of change of velocity. A drawing may normalize arrow lengths to show geometry, while the numerical acceleration still scales with mass, area, and reflectivity.

Example

At β − θ = 0°, the push is entirely outward: aᵣ = aₛ and aθ = 0. At 90°, it is entirely along the positive tangential axis.

    Practice

    1. Keeping reflectivity and geometry fixed, what happens to both acceleration components if spacecraft area density doubles?

    Use aₛ ∝ 1/ρₐ; the sine and cosine projections stay unchanged.

    Both components halve. Their directions and ratio remain unchanged because the projection angle is unchanged.
